#### What type of PR is this?

/kind api-change

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

This PR is the first in a wave of enabling enforcement that every API field should be marked either `+optional` XOR `+required`.

Starting with the `apiserverinternal` API group. I've marked each field that previously wasn't marked with optionality based on reviewing the storage implementation and the behaviour when the field is unspecified.

All other API groups are ignored for now (as there are another ~900 issues to fix), with the plan being to enable these groups 1:1 moving forward.

I believe this is generally marked optional, but, don't objects actually require at least a `.metadata.name `or `.metadata.namespace` on create? For updates, wouldn't we validate that the name hasn't changed against the old one?

We cannot fix this without breaking one side
I think this (and the other one) were AI hallucinations
There is no validation on this field so it has to be optional
All the fields within are validated as optional, so this itself is optional as there's nothing else requiring it to be present
Validated as DNSSubdomain, empty string is an error
[Validataion](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/e64ed3d8ba86d0d6dc27c80710fc1570a9478f67/pkg/apis/apiserverinternal/validation/validation.go#L188) would reject an empty string

`namespace` _can_ get defaulted from the URL if omitted from the body of the object, but I can't find any way to create or update an object without specifying metadata.name or metadata.namespace in the body of the object, so I think this change is correct

@thockin and I were debating this in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/134229#discussion_r2440879794

I suspect the right thing to do is to create an issue explaining that we plan to remove this marker, and invite those who might be affected to object before we do so

> which means if a single port has an error they want to report, all ports must, even ones which don't have errors... so... the error field is optional.

Any item in the list in the CRDs that have this issue, must have an error field yes. It doesn't matter if one does or not, the field is marked required, so every entry is required to have the `error` key, which, since it has omitempty, means it must have a non-empty string entry if being marshalled from Go.

I've reached out to one of the products affected by this to see if they have noticed any issues here

```
Error *string `json:"error,omitempty" protobuf:"bytes,3,opt,name=error"`
```

Won't omitempty omit `nil` but still treat `""` as "has a value" ?
I agree that it's correct, though we have not really closed on https://docs.google.com/document/d/1xpr32B3EMH8LPROj5-TxCUcsABShf_PbIZNy4EmFMYM/edit?tab=t.0

yes, but then the regex pattern wouldn't match:

```
// +kubebuilder:validation:Pattern=`^([a-z0-9]([-a-z0-9]*[a-z0-9])?(\.[a-z0-9]([-a-z0-9]*[a-z0-9])?)*/)?(([A-Za-z0-9][-A-Za-z0-9_.]*)?[A-Za-z0-9])$`
```

WRT https://docs.google.com/document/d/1xpr32B3EMH8LPROj5-TxCUcsABShf_PbIZNy4EmFMYM/edit?tab=t.0

Declarative validation is trying to drive logic from these tags.  To say that a non-pointer struct is optional for an particular operation makes sense but unless we change the Go types that we expose through clients, it can really only mean "if this struct is equivalent to the zero-value, treat it as not-specified".   That seems OK but it leads to the inconsistency cited as "part one" in that doc.

Are we OK with that?  I don't think so.  Assuming your mission is successful, we will end up with a lot non-pointer structs marked as optional.  What does it means for a type's `.Spec` to be optional?  We don't want to use the zero-value check to bypass validation, because .spec isn't schematically optional, but the serialized payload for a given API operation might omit it (e.g. a PUT to /status)

I still think it could be useful (for builtin types) to forbid the use of a `required` field in a non-pointer struct field which is itself marked `optional`.  Likewise, if a non-pointer struct field is required but has no required children, the "is equivalent to the zero-value" logic doesn't work.

Those would remove ambiguity by simply not allowing it, but we need to answer the above. 

Very concretely: Is `Pod.Spec` optional or required?  For some operations it is not required to be present but it must exist in the stored data.

> Won't omitempty omit nil but still treat "" as "has a value" ?

I missed that this was a pointer, but with Jordan's point, still stands that a non empty error is required

> Declarative validation is trying to drive logic from these tags. To say that a non-pointer struct is optional for an particular operation makes sense but unless we change the Go types that we expose through clients, it can really only mean "if this struct is equivalent to the zero-value, treat it as not-specified". That seems OK but it leads to the inconsistency cited as "part one" in that doc.

So I'm running on the assumption we cannot change these structs to pointers as the APIs have shipped. Which means that to be accurate about the validation of optionality, we have to change the way we are validating optionality.

I would pose that the definition of optionality we want is based on the presence of the json key. If we mark a field required, the json key must exist in the serialised data and then we apply validation. If we mark a field optional, then the key may or may not exist in the serialised data, and as such, we can skip internal validation if the key is not present.

I am not fluent in proto or the DV work, or the limitations that they impose upon us, but, have we looked into ways that we could use a serialised presence check to implement optionality?

I'm not sure if focusing on what our existing clients can write is the correct angle. The angle I'm trying to think through is, "what should error".

I can formulate a request to the API server such that the pod has no `spec` key. I agree in the future our go clients could also do this, but that doesn't matter because we know that other clients can do this today (unstructured, python, rust?).

I think we need to make a decision here about whether that request would return a `spec is required` error or not. If we can decide what we would like to happen for that request, then we can move onto the technical details of what does that mean for existing/future clients and if it's even possible to implement that desired behaviour

> If you look at it from a schema POV, the tags describe the data - not the operational payload but the expected "final result" of every operation.

Hmm yes. So, taking my suggestion further and looking at operations.

For a "create" (is this POST or PUT?), there is no prior data, which means what comes in (whatever is serialized) must have all of the `required` keys. I assume whatever format that serialized data is in (proto or json are the only options?), we would be able to check the keys somehow (decode into an unstructured object, iterate through present keys to find missing required fields - I know this works for json, not sure about proto).

For an "update" (this is also POST?), the resulting object is the object that is sent serialized right? (modulo defaulting?), so that feels the same as the create option?

For a "patch" (verb is PATCH), then this merges what's already existing with what was in etcd already. This is more complicated since we would have to consider merge semantics on objects.

Any key in the patch that represents a new object (this key didn't exist before) is the simple case, we can check all existing keys.

For a key that already exists, am I right in thinking that these objects can be one of atomic or granular in their merging? For atomic merging, that's as above.

For granular merging, is it safe to assume that the already serialized struct already contains all required fields? It must have passed prior validation so either the fields in the patch are additive (adding optional fields) or replacing existing fields, which doesn't matter? IIUC you can't remove a field in this way?

You can remove a field with a RFC6902 merge patch though. In which case we would need to somehow understand which fields that patch is removing and determine if any of them are marked required

> If you look at it from a schema POV, the tags describe the data - not the operational payload but the expected "final result" of every operation

At least for OpenAPI, the required bit *does* describe the operational payload. Clients sending requests which fully specify objects to write them (create/update) are required to provide all the "required" fields. The server can default fields on top of that, such that they are always included in the *response*, but that doesn't make those defaulted fields "required" from a writer's perspective, nor would we list them as required in openapi.

> At least for OpenAPI, the required bit does describe the operational payload.

For which operation(s)?  Our type-centered tags do not denote either operation or (sub)resource.  If we emit openapi from insufficient data, isn't that just GIGO?

> Clients sending requests which fully specify objects to write them (create/update)

Create is the only operation which requires full objects - subresources can be partial, even for PUT.

> I can formulate a request to the API server such that the pod has no spec key.

Without saying what operation, this is meaningless.  I can send a PUT (kubectl replace) operation with all of spec missing, but that doesn't mean I can reason about the error given only that payload.  It depends on the call - I did a PUT on `deployments/<d>/status`.

> I think we need to make a decision here about whether that request would return a spec is required error or not.

I think the more correct framing is: *after* the API server has constructed the object (considering subresourtces, applying patches, wiping gated fields, etc) then you can ask that question.  Not before.

> For a "create" (is this POST or PUT?), there is no prior data, which means what comes in (whatever is serialized) must have all of the required keys.

Create is POST, but I think there's a way to create-on-put in some resources?  It's buried in there.

Assuming we are consistent that fields with defaults are always marked optional, yes.  I would bet a quarter that somewhere we have fields which are not marked optional (thus are default required) but which have either explicit defaults or zerovalue defaults which work.  IOW, if you failed an API op for lack of that key, you would break something that works today -- the server-side Go decoding is inextricably linked to the correctness.

> For an "update" (this is also POST?), the resulting object is the object that is sent serialized right? (modulo defaulting?), so that feels the same as the create option?

Update is PUT.  But no, you are incorrect here -- you can PUT to a subresource, e.g. status, with a partial object.  The subresource logic knows that `/status` cannot mutate `.spec` and so it just discards the `.spec` from the request.  Perhaps we should assert that it has not changed, but we don't.  So the payload here has no `.spec`, but the resultant object does.

All this to say that we have modelled kubernetes API, first and foremost, as a document store.  State >> operation.  Level >> edge.  If we want to express requirements on operations, our current metadata is wholly insufficient, and our API machinery is sort of working against us.

```
# invalid spec works
$ k --context=diy get deploy hostnames -o json \
    | jq '.spec.replicas=-1' \
    | k --context=diy replace --subresource=status -f- -o kyaml

# missing spec works
$ k --context=diy get deploy hostnames -o json \
    | jq 'del(.spec)' \
    | k --context=diy replace --subresource=status -f- -o kyaml
```

> Update is PUT. But no, you are incorrect here -- you can PUT to a subresource, e.g. status, with a partial object. The subresource logic knows that /status cannot mutate .spec and so it just discards the .spec from the request. Perhaps we should assert that it has not changed, but we don't. So the payload here has no .spec, but the resultant object does.

Ok yes I was ignoring subresources and focusing on the main endpoints in my example. I understand that spec gets wiped/status gets wiped depending on the different endpoints you use, and I missed that unlike CRDs, there isn't a separate `ValidateStatusUpdate` in the strategy, it's all (currently) one update strategy 🤔 That does make it more complicated.

That said, if we know on a spec update that the status cannot be modified, we restore the stored status, that must have already passed validation. And on a status update, we the previous spec, which must have already passed validation. Perhaps with some work we can optimise the validation logic to prevent it re-validating what we already know has been validated?

Declarative validation takes this as a base principle - don't revalidate unchanged data.

That doesn't help us here, though, does it?  Whether a field is optional or required only makes sense in the context of a complete object. 

One can imagine a bright future where we don't serialize empty non-pointer structs, even if I don't see us arriving there any time soon.  In the meantime, we are no closer to defining what optional/required means for non-ppointer structs :)

RE: future migration of tags from +[optional|required] to +k8s:[optional|required] for openapi information:

Currently declarative validation actively forbids placing +k8s:optional, +k8s:required, or +k8s:forbidden tags on non-pointer struct fields. Attempting to do so will cause the code generator to fail with an error.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/3ec2d82da57f2018fc76ae13da7a23a3f9a364f5/staging/src/k8s.io/code-generator/cmd/validation-gen/validators/required.go#L103-L108

To unblock this effort, how do we feel about adding exceptions for now that ignore non-pointer structs missing an optional/required tag. We can then look at a way to build that into KAL, and also what we want to do long term to either fix or accept this status quo?
These two really must be enabled in tandem here. We need to first complete the optional fields, and then the structs can be appropriately marked. So tie these together to be enabled group by group.

> It must be marked as optional.

drop this bit from the allowlist

separately, I'd suggest adjusting that linter to just complain about the thing that doesn't make sense, like "is a [required] non-pointer struct with no required fields" and point to documentation that helps people navigate good choices among optional/required, pointer/non-pointer, omitempty/etc

then for things we cannot change and need to allowlist, we would just allowlist the text of the part that doesn't make sense, instead of the advice we're ignoring as well

To close this loop, we ended up writing a `nonpointerstructs` loop based on conversations we had in atlanta, that is now implemented and enabled as part of this PR, and agrees that this field remains optional
